body_paragraphs: The overnight round hardened rather than cooled. Hours after the US launched a 'heavy wave' of new strikes on Iran - killing at least three civilians, the first confirmed deaths of this specific round - and Iran hit back at Jordan and Kuwait, Qatar issued a formal condemnation of Tehran's strikes on its neighbors. That's the first real diplomatic isolation this round has produced, and it narrows Iran's room just as its military options are also narrowing.

The Fed's split vote kept doing damage into Thursday morning. Wednesday's hold, with three regional presidents dissenting for a hike, was bad enough; Meta's earnings miss - a legal-and-severance-driven shortfall paired with a guide toward $130-145B in AI spending this year - gave the market a second reason to worry. Equities are trying to bounce (futures up Thursday morning), but the bond market isn't buying the calm: the 30-year hit a multidecade high near 5.24%, and odds of a hike at the next meeting jumped to roughly 54%, up from 38% before Wednesday's vote.

Miami had a quieter, better day. The Marlins open at the Mets tonight fresh off their biggest comeback of the season; Dolphins camp added two good details - a rookie safety picking off his old college teammate, a pass rusher who reported to camp carrying real added muscle. And if you want an evening further from vote counts: a walk through why Hohauser's 1935 Colony Hotel still reads as radical, or an essay asking whether a Stoic's private calm is actually enough when the decisions that matter are being made by someone else's institution.

rabbit_hole.title: When Stoicism Is a Political, Not Just a Personal, Virtue
rabbit_hole.creator: Aeon Essays
rabbit_hole.why: Today handed you a vote count from the Fed and a retaliation ordered from someone else's war room - decisions other people made without you, that you now just have to metabolize. This essay takes on the standard critique of Stoicism head-on: that private equanimity is a philosophy for people who've opted out of changing anything, and asks whether that charge actually holds up.

beautiful_thing.title: The Colony Hotel
beautiful_thing.creator: Henry Hohauser, architect
beautiful_thing.body: Hohauser designed the Colony as the first genuinely 'streamlined' building on Ocean Drive - fifty rooms, each with its own private bathroom, wrapped in banded teal stripes separating three floors of glass. Its neon sign, black lettering on lilac glass mounted on an inverted T, still dominates the block. Where earlier Miami Beach hotels borrowed Mediterranean Revival ornament, the Colony borrowed its lines from ocean liners - the aerodynamic curves and porthole windows that would come to define the whole district. Other architects noticed almost immediately and followed.

noticing_prompt.text: Before you check a market number today, notice what you already expect it to say - then see whether the actual number changes your plan, or just confirms what you'd already decided to believe.

daily_puzzle.prompt: Three envelopes sit on a desk, labeled $10, $20, and $50. Each envelope actually contains one of those three amounts, and every single label is wrong - no envelope's label matches what's inside it. You may open exactly one envelope before you must state, with certainty, the true contents of all three. Which envelope do you open, and how does opening just that one tell you all three?
daily_puzzle.hint: Open the envelope labeled $10 - the rule already tells you it can't contain $10, so it starts with only two possibilities instead of three.
daily_puzzle.solution: Open the envelope labeled $10. Say it turns out to contain $20 (the reasoning mirrors if it held $50 instead). Since every label is wrong, the envelope labeled $50 can't hold $50, and it can't hold $20 either since that's already accounted for - so it must hold $10. That leaves the envelope labeled $20 to hold the only amount left over: $50.
daily_puzzle.explanation: With three items and a rule that no label matches its contents, one confirmed fact plus the 'no self-match' constraint leaves only one possible arrangement for the other two.

threads.title: Miami Marine Stadium's restoration referendum
threads.current_state: Miami voters decide Marine Stadium's future in an August 18 referendum (Referendum #172) on a 40-year management deal with Global Spectrum/Oak View Group and local partner Breakwater Hospitality. Under the deal, the city keeps 93% of event revenue and 85% of sponsorship income, with up to $10M toward restoration up front, followed by a separate $65-85M restoration bond. Early voting runs August 3-16; partial pile and seating repairs are already underway with county and state grant money.
